Package overview

Source: vignettes/package_overview/package_overview.Rmd
package_overview.Rmd

This article should give an overview of the existing articles (tutorials) described on the package website, compare what has changed in the basic workflow from atlastools, describe the sources of external data used and how to setup the working environment for internal WATLAS users.

Articles overview

The articles of the package are grouped by purpose. The basic workflow covers the steps most users need to go from raw WATLAS data to clean tracks, and the extended workflow covers more specialised analyses. The visualization tutorials show how to plot and animate movement data. The package development articles explain how to contribute to tools4watlas and how to adapt it, for example by creating your own basemaps.

Parts of the articles marked with an asterisk (*) require bathymetry data. These data are too large to include in tools4watlas, so those parts do not run without access to them. For tidal data, the package only includes an example dataset. See access to data sections below for how to get the complete data.


Basic workflow (Vignettes):

  • Load and check data

  • Filter data - based on spatial boundaries, temporal specifications, error estimates and speed.

  • Smooth and thin data

Extended workflow:

  • Add tidal and bathymetry data - (*add bathymetry data)

  • Add residence patches

  • Interpolate data

  • Add sun and moon data

Visualization tutorials:

  • Create a basemap - (*Bathymetry basemap option)

  • Plot data - an important step between all stages to check the data.

  • Plot data in loop - quick way to make plots by tag ID.

  • Plot data faster

  • Plot data interactively

  • Animate data - (*Animation with dynamic water data)

Package development:

  • Contributing to tools4watlas - describes how to work on tools4watlas.

  • Extract basemap data - describes how the basemap data were extracted and can guide the user in creating customized base maps.

  • tools4watlas logo - describes how the tools4watlas logo is made.

Differences from atlastools

tools4watlas builds on atlastools (Gupte et al. 2021. A Guide to Pre-processing High-throughput Animal Tracking Data) and incorporates basic data processing functions from it.

The main change is the data structure of the workflow: all functions now work on a single data.table and group by tag ID internally, while atlastools works on lists of data, with one element per individual. This list approach means that all functions have to be run with lapply(), which makes the code harder to read and working with the data more complicated in general. For example, to plot the data with ggplot2 in between, the data need to be combined or individuals added in loops to the plot. Switching back and forth between lists and a full table also copies the data in memory, which removes the benefit of data.table, which can modify data in place. This matters, because one season of WATLAS data can already be as big as 10 GB.

Comparison of basic workflow of tools4watlas and atlastools

The comparison covers three steps of the basic workflow: calculating speed, smoothing, and thinning the data.

First we load packages and raw example data.

# packages
library(tools4watlas)
library(data.table)

# path to csv with raw data
data_path <- system.file(
  "extdata", "watlas_data_raw.csv",
  package = "tools4watlas"
)

# load data
data <- fread(data_path, yaml = TRUE)

tools4watlas

The full data.table is used by the function group by tag ID.

# calculate speed
data <- atl_get_speed(data, type = c("in", "out"))

# smooth the data
data <- atl_median_smooth(data, moving_window = 5)

# thin data
data_thinned <- atl_thin_data(
  data,  interval = 60, id_columns = c("tag", "species"), method = "aggregate"
)

atlastools

Example workflow with atlastools. The data.table must first be split by tag ID, and every function is then run on each element with lapply(). The split creates a full copy of the data, so the data are held in memory twice.

# split data by tag ID
data_split <- split(data, by = "tag")

# calculate speed
lapply(data_split, function(dt) {
  dt[, `:=`(
    speed_in  = atlastools::atl_get_speed(dt, time = "time", type = "in"),
    speed_out = atlastools::atl_get_speed(dt, time = "time", type = "out")
  )]
})

# smooth data
lapply(
  X = data_split,
  FUN = atlastools::atl_median_smooth,
  x = "x",
  y = "y",
  time = "time",
  moving_window = 5
)

# thin data
data_thinned <- lapply(
  X = data_split,
  FUN = atlastools::atl_thin_data,
  interval = 60,
  time = "time",
  id_columns = c("tag", "species"),
  method = "aggregate"
)

Benchmark both basic workflows

I simply wrapped both workflows as shown above and used mark from the bench package to compare them. The code is not shown again, but can be seen on GitHub

# benchmark
result <- bench::mark(
  tools4watlas = workflow_tools4watlas(data),
  atlastools   = workflow_atlastools(data),
  iterations = 5,
  check = FALSE,
  filter_gc = FALSE
)

# print results
result[, c("expression", "min", "median", "mem_alloc", "n_gc")] |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
expression min median mem_alloc n_gc
tools4watlas 47.4ms 58.9ms 60MB 13
atlastools 472ms 481.1ms 58.9MB 34

The workflow of tools4watlas is around 10x faster using this small example. When we run the same comparison for a larger data set of 300 individuals and ~3 GB (not shown), the speed is even 25x times faster.

Comparison of residence patch analysis of tools4watlas and atlastools

The residence patch function was modified in tools4watlas. It now returns the original table with a patch column instead of a summary with nested data, and patch summaries are created separately with atl_res_patch_summary(). Proto-patches are built with a speed threshold (max_speed) in addition to distance and time thresholds, which replaces the buffer radius, and they are merged when either their median positions or their end and start positions are close. The function also fills gaps within patches, splits patches at flights, removes single outliers, and can filter patches by minimum duration (min_duration) as well as by number of fixes.

Residence patches are too complex to calculate for all tags at once, so this step still has to be done per tag ID. In tools4watlas, we use foreach, which makes it easy to switch to parallel processing with doFuture (see Add residence patches).

tools4watlas 

# packages
library(foreach)

# tag IDs to loop through
id <- unique(data$tag)

# loop through all tags to calculate residence patches
data <- foreach(i = id, .combine = "rbind") %do% {
  atl_res_patch(
    data[tag == i],
    max_speed = 3, lim_spat_indep = 75, lim_time_indep = 180,
    min_fixes = 2, min_duration = 60
  )
}

# patch summaries are created separately
data_summary <- atl_res_patch_summary(data)

atlastools 

# atlastools::atl_res_patch() requires an "id" column
lapply(data_split, function(dt) dt[, id := tag])

# calculate residence patches per tag ID
patches <- lapply(
  X = data_split,
  FUN = atlastools::atl_res_patch,
  buffer_radius = 10,
  lim_spat_indep = 100,
  lim_time_indep = 30,
  min_fixes = 3,
  summary_variables = c("speed_in"),
  summary_functions = c("mean", "sd")
)

As a result the get a summary table with all patch data nested in one column.

# one row per patch, localisations nested in `patchdata`
patches <- rbindlist(patches)

# to get the localisations with patch ID again, the data must be unnested
data_patches <- patches[,
  unlist(patchdata, recursive = FALSE),
  by = .(id, patch)
]

# add the patch ID to the original table
data[data_patches, on = .(tag, time), patch := i.patch]

Benchmark both residence patch workflows

I simply wrapped both residence patch workflows as shown above and used mark from the bench package to compare them. The code is not shown again, but can be seen on GitHub

# benchmark
result <- bench::mark(
  tools4watlas = workflow_tools4watlas(data),
  atlastools   = workflow_atlastools(data),
  iterations = 5,
  check = FALSE,
  filter_gc = FALSE
)

# print results
result[, c("expression", "min", "median", "mem_alloc", "n_gc")] |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
expression min median mem_alloc n_gc
tools4watlas 1.46s 1.57s 323MB 23
atlastools 8.94s 9.13s 893MB 37

The workflow of tools4watlas is around 5x faster using this small example. When we run the same comparison for a larger data set of 10 random tags (not shown), it remains 5 times faster, but also allocates 70% less memory. When we use %dofuture%, it runs 17x faster.

Data access for external users

  • Tidal data: Are downloaded from Rijkswaterstaat for each tidal station and pre-processed to assign tide ID, high tide and low tide. Please contact Allert Bijleveld for access.
  • Bathymetry data: The data can be downloaded from the Waddenregister, to link them directly, they need to be opened with terra and the projection needs to be changed to UTM31 (EPSG:32631). To get processed ready to use data contact Allert Bijleveld

Data access and setup for internal WATLAS data users

Section only relevant for users with access to the local NIOZ network.

To work safely with database credentials and internal file paths, store them as environment variables in R. This way, scripts can be shared on GitHub without publishing credentials or personal paths. To add the variables, open your .Renviron file with usethis::edit_r_environ(), add one line per variable, save the file, and restart R. The all scripts should then run without further changes if all paths are correct.

The following variables are used:

  • Host, username and password are required to access the remote SQL database. Contact Allert Bijleveld for access.
  • watlas_teams: path to the “WATLAS” SharePoint folder Documents/data/. It contains files that are updated often, such as tags_watlas_all.xlsx and the tide data. We recommend adding a shortcut to this folder in your OneDrive, so that changes are synchronised automatically, and pointing the variable to this copy.
  • rasters: path to the “Birds, fish ’n chips” SharePoint folder Documents/data/GIS/rasters/.
  • shapefiles: path to the “Birds, fish ’n chips” SharePoint folder Documents/data/GIS/shapefiles/. These GIS folders contain many large files that rarely change. We recommend copying only the data you need to a local folder and pointing the variables to that folder, instead of creating a OneDrive shortcut.
  • sqlite_db: path to the folder with the SQLite localization databases.

To build the package website (see Contributing to tools4watlas) with all articles, all variables must be set.

Here a code template to fill the .Renviron: 

# open .Renviron to edit
usethis::edit_r_environ()

# add variables
host = "host"
username = "username"
password = "password"
watlas_teams = "file_path"
rasters = "file_path"
shapefiles = "file_path"
sqlite_db = "file_path"

# access variables (example)
Sys.getenv("variable_name")

Here templates to access the data (to replace in articles that use example data):

Metadata tags_watlas_all.xlsx:

# file path to WATLAS teams data folder
fp <- Sys.getenv("watlas_teams")

# load meta data
all_tags <- readxl::read_excel(
  paste0(fp, "tags/tags_watlas_all.xlsx"),
  sheet = "tags_watlas_all"
) |>
  data.table()

Tidal data:

# file path to WATLAS teams data folder
fp <- Sys.getenv("watlas_teams")

# sub path to tide data
tidal_pattern_fp <- paste0(
  fp, "waterdata/allYears-tidalPattern-west_terschelling-UTC.csv"
)
measured_water_height_fp <- paste0(
  fp, "waterdata/allYears-gemeten_waterhoogte-west_terschelling-clean-UTC.csv"
)

# load tide data
tidal_pattern <- fread(tidal_pattern_fp)
measured_water_height <- fread(measured_water_height_fp)

Bathymetry data:

# file path to Birds, fish 'n chips GIS/rasters folder
fp <- Sys.getenv("rasters")

# load bathymetry data
bat <- rast(paste0(fp, "bathymetry/2024/bodemhoogte_20mtr_UTM31_int.tif"))
